summary: Defines objects for managing AppleTalk networks with SNMP. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 1742.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a checklist for watching networks that use Apple's older networking system.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for AppleTalk networks

tldr.problem: AppleTalk networks needed a standard way to be monitored and managed using SNMP, the Internet's network management protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of managed objects organized into groups covering AppleTalk's protocols and services: address resolution, routing, datagram delivery, naming, and network connectivity.
tldr.outcome: This provides a complete MIB for managing AppleTalk networks in mixed IP and AppleTalk environments. It was later replaced by RFC 1742 with an updated version.

facts.value: 9 types including LocalTalk, EtherTalk, TokenTalk, IPTalk

today: RFC 1243 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1742, which provides an updated version of the AppleTalk MIB. The newer RFC updates and extends the definitions to reflect subsequent experience with AppleTalk network management.

sections.title: Introduction to AppleTalk MIB
sections.content:
RFC 1243 defines the Management Information Base (MIB) for AppleTalk networks. A MIB is a collection of data objects that can be read and sometimes modified by network management systems using SNMP. This RFC creates a standard way for Apple's AppleTalk protocol suite to be managed on the same management infrastructure used by Internet protocols.

AppleTalk is a peer-to-peer protocol suite that runs over various transmission media. As organizations built large AppleTalk networks alongside Internet networks, they needed a way to manage both using the same tools. This RFC provides that capability by defining managed objects for the key AppleTalk protocols and services.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a rulebook that says which numbers a network manager can ask to see about an AppleTalk network, and what each number means.

sections.title: AppleTalk Protocol Groups
sections.content:
The MIB is organized into nine protocol groups, each representing a major component of the AppleTalk protocol suite:

LLAP (LocalTalk Link Access Protocol) handles the low-cost data-link layer for LocalTalk connections, a medium-speed protocol designed for simple plug-and-play networks. AARP (AppleTalk Address Resolution Protocol) maps AppleTalk addresses to underlying data-link layer addresses. AppleTalk Port manages the logical connections that allow AppleTalk packets to be transmitted. DDP (Datagram Delivery Protocol) is the network layer responsible for datagram delivery. RTMP (Routing Table Maintenance Protocol) maintains the routing tables that direct packets through an AppleTalk internet.

KIP (Kinetics Internet Protocol) encapsulates and routes AppleTalk datagrams over IP networks. ZIP (Zone Information Protocol) maintains mappings between networks and zone names for name lookup. NBP (Name Binding Protocol) converts human-readable service names into numeric AppleTalk addresses. AppleTalk Echo Protocol tests and verifies the status of the AppleTalk internet.
sections.plainLanguage: AppleTalk has many separate parts that do different jobs. This document creates a measurement for each one, so managers can check that all the parts are working.

sections.title: DDP Addresses and Interfaces
sections.content:
AppleTalk addresses have a specific format: they consist of three octets encoding a two-octet network number in network byte order, followed by a one-octet node number. This 3-octet format, called a DDP Address, uniquely identifies a device on an AppleTalk network.

An AppleTalk Port is a logical connection to a network over which AppleTalk packets can be transmitted. Each port can be configured for different AppleTalk port types, including LocalTalk, EtherTalk (versions 1 and 2), TokenTalk for token-ring networks, IPTalk for IP encapsulation, and various serial configurations. The MIB allows configuration and monitoring of each port's network address range, status, and zone information.
sections.plainLanguage: Each AppleTalk device has a three-number address. A port is like a network connection card in a computer, and the MIB lets you see what kind of connection it is and what network numbers it handles.

sections.title: Data Delivery and Routing
sections.content:
The DDP group defines counters for tracking datagram traffic: outgoing requests, short and long datagrams transmitted, incoming datagrams received, and datagrams forwarded to other networks. It also tracks error conditions such as datagrams that are too short or too long, datagrams with no route, and broadcast datagrams destined for destinations other than the receiving system.

RTMP maintains routing tables that allow AppleTalk routers to forward datagrams correctly. The MIB provides access to routing information and maintains statistics on how RTMP operates. LLAP statistics track collisions, transmission deferrals, and frame check sequence errors at the link layer.
sections.plainLanguage: DDP is like the postal service, carrying messages from one place to another. RTMP is like a map that routers use to know which way to send packets. The MIB counts how many packets go through, how many get lost, and what errors happen.

sections.title: Network Management Framework
sections.content:
This MIB is part of the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which consists of three components. RFC 1155 defines the Structure of Management Information (SMI), the language and rules for describing managed objects. RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for Internet protocols. RFC 1157 defines SNMP, the protocol used for accessing managed objects over the network.

The objects defined in this RFC follow these standards and can be accessed using any standard SNMP management application. Implementations of this MIB should provide read access to all objects, and some objects (such as port configuration and status) are defined as read-write to allow network operators to manage the AppleTalk network remotely.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB follows the same rules that all Internet network management uses. Any management software that understands those rules can use it to talk to AppleTalk networks.
